title: forget "why buy your game". why would i even play it, if i can make my own in a weekend?
author: FotoRe_store
selftext:
i keep seeing posts here about wishlists, steam pages, kickstarters, "how do i get players". feels like most of us are still thinking in the old world. its not that ai makes games easier to make. its that the whole idea of "a game for players" is changing.

look what people actually post here. "my daughter asked for cute bees so i made a bee game". "made it so i could play it". "my dream game with all my favorite features". games made for one person or one family. thats already the new normal.

and with this speed, very soon anyone with a bit of fantasy will just make the game they want to play, exactly how they want it. and then they wont have time for games made by strangers at all. maybe a friends game, maybe their kids game, thats it. same thing that happened to photos. everyone takes them now, and nobody even looks at strangers photos, only friends and family.

so be honest, do you still play other peoples games since you started making your own? and if not, who are we all making games for?

replies.author: Creepy-Pain3449
replies.body:
Most people are not playing every single game in existence. They pick the best of bests, even in smaller niches, and play those. Good quality games only get the recognition they deserve, and even for an AI game like Slotbound, it is only getting recognition because the dev spent months polishing the game and replacing placeholders with paid assets to get it up to a standard worth playing. 

Most mobile games are not worth playing, but there will always be a few standouts. Quality no matter how it is made, will always matter. No one will play slop or prototypes because someone using AI can whip out a game in an afternoon and think that is presentable or acceptable to a wider audience

replies.author: teapot_RGB_color
replies.body:
I've spent some not insignificant time with AI writing. While it's doing some good groundwork, I eventually had to go in and rewrite every single sentence.

It's due to the way AI works, it falls back on "what is most likely", so you'll end up with a bunch of cliche stuff. I think you'll understand when you start reading.. It keep arriving at the same predictable destination unless it's steered to a degree where you are writing the content yourself.

replies.author: Crunchfest3

You can build exactly the game you asked for, but you also know what is behind every door and why each clue exists. Someone else's decisions can take you somewhere you wouldn't have thought to build yourself. Making games easier to create doesn't remove that reason to play them.

comments.author: niloony
comments.body:

Many people don't want to make something because they know someone else can make something much better and they can pay them a bit of money to get access to it. That doesn't change with AI, in a world where people are making games they want to play.

A good book, movie or game gives you something that you didn't know you wanted or could exist.

comments.author: Affectionate_Tie357

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: yeah "yet" is the key word for me. half a year ago what took me days now would take weeks, and in another half a year who knows. but you and the books comment have a point, i cant make silksong and probably wont soon, and some fun is in being surprised by someone elses idea. i think the big shift is that a lot of people who just wanted "a game like X but with Y" will make it themselves, and the stuff that stays worth playing will be the really deep authored games

A lot of you don’t want to hear it but just because this technology is making the technical side of gaming more accessible, doesn’t mean you also understand the game dev process such as iteration, testing, and failing.

comments.author: Opulon_Nelva
comments.body:
In the absolute theory, people may be able to do their fantasy game on their own.

In practice, I see several things (as a professional from the industry)

1) Ironically, the more AI tools become powerful, the less I'm worried about my own expertise. Many people have no clue why they like a game more than on a superficial level. Knowing it requires already a non insignificant and non distillable effort. 

2) Do you want to make games, or do you want to enjoy them ?  Even if AI becomes amazing at inferring tastes and desires. People will increase their own baselines, which will always require an effort they don't put, or money they can't invest. You will not enjoy experiences ''''you'''' have written in the same way. You will enjoy sharing them. 

( This is the trope of the expert baker : he makes the best croissants in the world, but he smells butter 24/24 and doesn't want to eat croissants)

3) people not looking at strangers photos/videos seem a bit questionable in the era of Tiktok. Our brains do crave discovery, billions are made daily out of our attention for novelty and trends. People are even looking at the AI content of others even if they can make it themselves already. 


4) The ambitions we put on AI has been growing quicker than its cost efficiency, right now. It may change.

I do not imagine though, even in case of successive cost efficiency breakthrough ( let's say -75% with constant quality), in our current world where the representative human earns 800 dollars net a month, he will be willing to put 50-60 of them a month + the free time, to generate his own custom entertainment.

Some will, of course, and that will expand as a hobby, which it already is.

Right now, though, to do your 'dream prototype of a game' and make it enjoyable for yourself more than a few minutes, you are on a 400 dollars a month personal budget and a shit ton metric of learning work to do.

Even prompting... The most basic and boring thing in the world... requires verbal intelligence and proficiency.

comments.author: YYS770
comments.body:
How about 3D printing? Why buy it if I can 3d print it? 

It's not quite at the same scale, but very similar in a way. In both cases (game design and 3d printing), the final product, although more easily attainable than in the past, still requires a LOT of effort and input to make it GOOD. Take for example the guy who makes board games as 3d-printable files you can buy, with the catch that each board game folds itself into a neat decorative item you can place around the house. No one can just model that in a CAD program and 3d print it... you still need tons of effort. Same with games - many, many, MANY details and their respective effort involved (see the next paragraph) in order to make a game that you will enjoy playing more than just a couple of times, whether you use AI or not. Such a game will be bought as a result of the effort put into it. 

Also, not everyone is that creative...So the type of people to actually go through the above-described process in order to actually put together a game is not that great. And aside from the hefty amount of creativity needed to create such a good game, in order to make it enjoyable you also have to incorporate a wealth of disciplines that are not easy at all to master. Certainly AI makes these disciplines MUCH more reachable for game designers (like UX and all its related fields - level design, UI design, and too many sub-fields to list here off the top of my head), but you still need a human to guide it along in order to make the vision actually playable and enjoyable.

comments.author: Impressive_Award_679

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: well now you heard of one lol. i was never really a gamer, and now the only game i play is the one im making. i just dont have time for anything else, every evening i test the new version with my own hand and then think what to change next. so yeah its not a big statistic, but im exactly that person

replies.author: Impressive_Award_679
replies.body:
But as you said: You never "really was a gamer". Maybe thats the point? Maybe you like testing and changing stuff more like a "dev" instead of a gamer. Which is totally fine. Dont get me wrong. I'm happy for you if you have fun doing so. But without sounding harsh, i'm pretty sure someone who wants to play games in the first place, wouldnt prefer currently or even in 2 years AI made games within a weekend. The quality difference is just to huge. Why should for example a Poe2 player play a absolutly unbalanced, unsecure, worse looking and feeling AI made game if Poe2 is a AAA game in nearly every aspect and also for free? Why should someone who wants to play a game waste his time on creating something 100 times worse instead of just downloading and playing? Because AI isnt free also. Making something decent looking right now with AI costs also some decent amount comparable to a game price. So you pay for something thats still alot worse than even a AA game, waste a weekend on it for what exactly? 

Game design and for sure balancing isnt something AI can do for you and if you try to make a big game, youre more testing and balancing stuff than actually enjoying it as a "gamer" in the first place. But most people just want to play a already balanced and good game. And thats nothing you can create in a weekend. Sure you migh be able to create a decent simple Tetris, a decent simple low poly tower defending game or ai looking card game or whatever. But nothing bigger that just comes 1% on the amount of content and quality of even a AA studio or indie artists that take their time and efford into game making.

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: yeah thats exactly my point actually. im not saying poe2 players will quit and build their own. im saying theres a new kind of player now, people like me who never cared about games and now spend every evening on this. for us the making is the game, and that game just didnt exist before. so we kind of agree lol

But your whole posts reads like you ask why people overall should still buy games when you just could make your own in weekend. And most gamers just like playing a good game. Thats just something AI cant deliver in a weekend.

comments.author: klas-klattermus
comments.body:
Because most people's capacity is like "make a game like GTA but it's super mario karts in mushroom kingdom" and you might get temu super mario throwing blue shells at cops in the mushroom kingdom, but then what?
How well should the blue shells steer, do they auto target closest enemy or the enemy you are aiming at or the enemy you aimed at when you fired? How do you get shells, what's a good cool down ratio for throwing shells, do you have different throwing strengths, is one hit enough to knock down an enemy, does enemies get back up eventually or do they die? Etc. 
You got to make design decisions otherwise it's not a comprehensive game, just a tech demo with random rules. And given AI if you express yourself wrongly it might affect other parts of the game unintentionally because of how it interpret you

comments.author: hunteel
comments.body: As absurd as saying nobody would read any blog because anyone could make his own blog

comments.author: accidentalfish_
comments.body:
The games I play are, and this is the key bit, well crafted. Whether the creator(s) have used AI or not they've been iterated on and you can feel it. I'm currently into "brown" FPS games. Finished Dusk recently and playing HROT at the moment. Fabulous games with real heart and soul to them. But they're not for everyone.

My hope for AI is that it makes it easier for talented people to create well-crafted games. So I can have more high quality brown shooters. Or whatever else I'm obsessing over at the time. While big studios will use it to make it cheaper for them to mass produce the slop most of them have been creating for the last 10 years.

The issue is going to be discoverability - finding these games amongst the slop. And as AI gets better that will be harder because it will create better store front focused facsimiles of things with real heart and soul to them.

To me the new world is that AI makes small teams, or individuals, iterate faster on game ideas and attempt things that previously would have been out of reach. I completed a 4X game recently. Even with AI its been a lot of work - that work hasn't been coding, but play testing, tuning, reworking systems, finding the fun. (Annhexation by the way, shameless plug: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4663920/Annhexation/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4663920/Annhexation/) ).

I mean maybe someone uses AI to create a cute bee game for their daughter. I'm sure they will. And that daughter might love it. But I see no signs that AI is able to "just create this game" and its fun and worth playing.

I'd also note that for all the "I used 100 agents to create this thing" there is a significant lack of proof of work. And when there is proof of work its utter dribble - like that thing Steve Yegge shared and weirdly seemed proud of. AI psychosis at work.

comments.author: meowyih

comments.author: GigaTerra
comments.body: No amount of AI will turn an person into an person into an gene engineer, that is to say AI can't make you into something you are not or have no understanding of. AI can ***help*** you make an game, that is all.
